column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which statement best describes mitosis?
column14: It makes a copy of all of the cell's DNA before the cell divides
column15: It makes sperm and egg cells that have half the usual number of chromosomes
column16: It splits the cytoplasm after the cell has already made two nuclei
column17: It splits one nucleus into two nuclei that each have an identical set of chromosomes
column28: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus: one nucleus becomes two, and each new nucleus gets an identical set of chromosomes. Copying the DNA happens earlier, during interphase, and splitting the cytoplasm is cytokinesis. Making sex cells is meiosis, which is the most common mix-up.
column29: Mitosis is only one part of cell division. Which part of the cell is it dividing?

column9: A typical body cell spends most of its life in which stage of the cell cycle?
column14: Prophase
column15: Cytokinesis
column16: Interphase
column17: Metaphase
column28: Cells spend about 90% of the cell cycle in interphase, growing, doing their normal jobs, and copying their DNA. Mitosis and cytokinesis are short by comparison. A common mistake is thinking a cell is dividing most of the time.
column29: Dividing is quick. Which stage is the cell in when it is simply living and working?

column9: The thin, loose form of DNA that is spread through the nucleus of a cell that is not dividing is called ___.
column28: Chromatin is DNA wrapped around proteins in a loose, spread-out form. It coils up tightly into chromosomes when the cell gets ready to divide. A common mistake is writing chromosome, which is the tightly coiled form.
column29: It is the same material as a chromosome, just uncoiled. The word starts with chroma-.

column9: During the ___ phase of interphase, the cell copies (replicates) all of its DNA.
column28: DNA is copied during the S (synthesis) phase. G1 comes before it and is mostly growth; G2 comes after and gets the cell ready to divide. A common mistake is saying DNA is copied during mitosis, but mitosis only separates copies that were already made.
column29: Interphase has three parts. The one in the middle is named for making (synthesizing) new DNA.

column9: Under the microscope, a student sees a cell whose chromosomes form a single line across the center of the cell. Which phase is this cell in?
column14: Prophase
column15: Telophase
column16: Anaphase
column17: Metaphase
column28: In metaphase the chromosomes line up across the middle (the equator) of the cell. In anaphase they are moving apart, and in telophase they are at the two ends. A memory trick: M for metaphase, M for middle.
column29: Think 'M' for middle.

column9: In which phase of mitosis do the two copies of each chromosome separate and get pulled toward opposite ends of the cell?
column14: Prophase
column15: Telophase
column16: Metaphase
column17: Anaphase
column28: In anaphase the copies of each chromosome separate and move to opposite poles. They lined up in metaphase just before this, and they arrive at the poles in telophase. A memory trick: A for anaphase, A for apart.
column29: Think 'A' for apart.

column9: In which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes reach opposite ends of the cell and a new nuclear membrane forms around each set?
column14: Telophase
column15: Prophase
column16: Interphase
column17: Metaphase
column28: Telophase is the last phase of mitosis. The chromosomes reach the poles, start to unwind, and a nuclear membrane forms around each group, making two nuclei. Prophase is the opposite: that is when the nuclear membrane breaks down.
column29: This phase is basically prophase run in reverse.

column9: In which phase of mitosis do the long, thin strands of DNA coil up into thick chromosomes that can first be seen with a light microscope?
column14: Prophase
column15: Telophase
column16: Metaphase
column17: Anaphase
column28: Prophase is the first phase of mitosis. The DNA coils (condenses) into thick, visible chromosomes, the nuclear membrane breaks down, and the spindle starts to form. A common mistake is choosing metaphase, but by then the chromosomes are already lined up.
column29: Which phase comes first, when the cell is just getting started?

column9: What happens during cytokinesis?
column14: New organelles are built inside the nucleus
column15: The DNA is copied
column16: The cytoplasm divides, forming two separate cells
column17: Two cells join together to form one larger cell
column28: Cytokinesis (cyto = cell, kinesis = movement) is the division of the cytoplasm. It finishes cell division by splitting one cell into two. Copying DNA happens in interphase, not cytokinesis.
column29: Cyto- means cell. What has to happen to the rest of the cell after the nucleus splits?

column9: When one cell finishes mitosis and cytokinesis, how many cells are there?
column28: One parent cell divides into 2 daughter cells. A common mistake is saying 4, which is the number of cells made by meiosis.
column29: The cell divides one time. One thing split once makes how many pieces?

column9: How do the two daughter cells made by mitosis compare with the parent cell?
column14: They have half as many chromosomes as the parent cell
column15: They are genetically identical to the parent cell
column16: They have twice as many chromosomes as the parent cell
column17: They have a mix of DNA from two different parents
column28: Mitosis gives each daughter cell an exact copy of the parent cell's chromosomes, so the cells are genetically identical. Having half the chromosomes or a mix of DNA from two parents describes meiosis and fertilization, not mitosis.
column29: The DNA was copied once and divided once. Did anything get added or lost?

column9: A duplicated chromosome is shaped like an X. What is each of the two identical halves of the X called?
column14: A chromatid
column15: A centriole
column16: A nucleolus
column17: A spindle fiber
column28: Each half of a duplicated chromosome is a chromatid. The two halves are called sister chromatids because they are identical copies. Centrioles and spindle fibers are parts of the machinery that moves chromosomes, not parts of the chromosome itself.
column29: The two halves are 'sisters.' Which word sounds like it is part of a chromosome?

column9: Which part of a duplicated chromosome holds its two identical halves together?
column14: The centriole
column15: The centromere
column16: The cell plate
column17: The cell membrane
column28: The centromere is the pinched-in spot where the two halves of a duplicated chromosome are joined. A very common mistake is mixing up centromere (on the chromosome) with centriole (a small structure that helps make the spindle in animal cells).
column29: It is at the center of the X. Both answers that start with 'centr-' sound alike, so read carefully.

column9: Which structures attach to the chromosomes and move them around the cell during mitosis?
column14: Vacuoles
column15: Spindle fibers
column16: The cell wall
column17: Ribosomes
column28: Spindle fibers are long protein fibers that attach to the chromosomes and pull them into line and then apart. Ribosomes make proteins, vacuoles store materials, and the cell wall supports plant cells; none of them move chromosomes.
column29: Picture ropes stretched from one end of the cell to the other.

column9: Mitosis does all but one of these jobs in the human body. Which job is NOT done by mitosis?
column14: Healing a broken bone
column15: Helping a baby grow bigger
column16: Replacing skin cells that rub off
column17: Making sperm and egg cells
column28: Sperm and egg cells are made by meiosis, which cuts the chromosome number in half. Growth, healing, and replacing worn-out cells all use mitosis to make identical body cells. Mixing up mitosis and meiosis is the most common mistake here.
column29: Which of these cells needs only half of the usual chromosomes?

column9: A soccer player scrapes her knee. Over the next week, new skin grows over the scrape. Which process made the new skin cells?
column14: Mitosis
column15: Photosynthesis
column16: Meiosis
column17: Fertilization
column28: Skin cells around the scrape divide by mitosis to make new, identical skin cells, which repairs the damage. Meiosis only makes sex cells, and fertilization joins a sperm and egg.
column29: The new cells need to be exact copies of the skin cells that were already there.

column9: In an animal cell, which small structures move to opposite ends of the cell during prophase and help organize the spindle fibers?
column14: Lysosomes
column15: Centrioles
column16: Centromeres
column17: Ribosomes
column28: Centrioles are small, tube-shaped structures (found inside the centrosome) that move to opposite poles and organize the spindle in animal cells. The centromere is the spot that joins the two halves of a chromosome, and mixing up these two look-alike words is the most common mistake.
column29: Not the one that is part of a chromosome. Look for the one that sits at the poles.

column9: Plant cells and animal cells both divide by mitosis.
column28: True. Plants and animals are both eukaryotes, so their cells have a nucleus and divide it by mitosis. The main difference shows up in cytokinesis, when plant cells build a new wall instead of pinching in. A common mistake is thinking plants grow some other way.
column29: Do plant cells have a nucleus?

column9: Which cells in your body are produced by mitosis?
column14: Only the cells in your brain
column15: None of them, because human cells do not divide
column16: Only sperm and egg cells
column17: Body (somatic) cells such as skin, muscle, and bone cells
column28: Somatic (body) cells, like skin, muscle, bone, and blood-forming cells, are made by mitosis. Sperm and egg cells are made by meiosis. A common mistake is thinking only certain organs use mitosis.
column29: Somatic means 'of the body.'

column9: In an animal cell, cytokinesis happens when the cell membrane pinches inward around the middle of the cell, forming a ___.
column28: Animal cells pinch in at the middle, forming a cleavage furrow, until the cell splits in two. Plant cells can't do this because of their stiff cell wall; they build a cell plate instead. Writing cell plate for an animal cell is the most common mistake.
column29: Picture a belt being pulled tighter and tighter around the middle. The groove has a special name.

column9: Put the four phases of mitosis in order, from first to last.
column14: Anaphase
column15: Telophase
column16: Metaphase
column17: Prophase
column28: The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT). Chromosomes appear, line up in the middle, pull apart, and then form two new nuclei. A common mistake is swapping metaphase and anaphase.
column29: Chromosomes have to line up in the middle before they can be pulled apart.

column9: Put these events of one full cell cycle in order, starting right after a new cell forms.
column14: The cytoplasm splits, making two cells
column15: The cell grows and does its normal job
column16: The cell makes extra proteins and organelles to get ready to divide
column17: The cell copies all of its DNA
column18: The nucleus divides into two nuclei
column28: G1 (growth) → S (DNA copied) → G2 (getting ready) → mitosis (nucleus divides) → cytokinesis (cytoplasm divides). A common mistake is putting DNA copying after the nucleus divides, but the DNA must be copied first so each new nucleus gets a full set.
column29: The DNA has to be copied before the nucleus can split, and the nucleus splits before the whole cell does.

column9: Match each phase of mitosis to what happens during it.
column14: Telophase :: The chromosomes start to unwind and the spindle breaks down
column15: Prophase :: The spindle begins to form and the nuclear membrane breaks apart
column16: Metaphase :: Spindle fibers hold the chromosomes in a row at the cell's equator
column17: Anaphase :: Each chromosome's two copies are dragged toward opposite poles
column28: Prophase sets up (spindle forms, nuclear membrane breaks down), metaphase lines up, anaphase pulls apart, and telophase rebuilds two nuclei. Mixing up prophase and telophase is common because they are opposites.
column29: Use PMAT: set up, line up, pull apart, rebuild.

column9: A fruit fly body cell has 8 chromosomes. After it goes through mitosis, how many chromosomes will each daughter cell have?
column28: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, so each daughter cell gets 8 chromosomes, just like the parent. The DNA was copied before mitosis, so there is a full set for each cell. Choosing 4 is the common mistake of confusing mitosis with meiosis.
column29: Mitosis makes cells that are copies of the parent cell.

column9: A puppy grows into a full-size dog. How does mitosis make this growth possible?
column14: It mixes DNA from both parents into every new cell
column15: It joins small cells together into larger cells
column16: It increases the number of cells in the dog's body
column17: It makes each of the puppy's cells grow to a huge size
column28: Animals grow mainly by making more cells, not bigger cells. Mitosis and cytokinesis turn one cell into two, again and again. A common mistake is thinking cells just keep getting bigger, but cells have a size limit.
column29: An adult dog's cells are about the same size as a puppy's. So what is different?

column9: A brand-new liver cell is growing and making the proteins it needs to do its job. It has not copied its DNA yet. Which phase is it in?
column14: G2
column15: G1
column16: S
column17: Metaphase
column28: G1 is the first part of interphase, right after a cell is made. The cell grows and does its normal work. S comes next (DNA copied), then G2. A common mistake is choosing G2, which happens after the DNA has been copied.
column29: The DNA has not been copied yet, so the cell is in the part of interphase that comes before that step.

column9: A cell has just finished copying its DNA. It is now making extra organelles and the proteins it will need to divide. Which phase is it in?
column14: S
column15: G1
column16: Anaphase
column17: G2
column28: G2 is the last part of interphase. The DNA is already copied, and the cell makes the proteins and organelles it needs before mitosis. A common mistake is choosing S, but S is when the copying happens, and that is already done.
column29: Which part of interphase comes after the DNA copying is finished?

column9: Which of these are examples of mitosis at work? Select all that apply.
column14: A raisin swelling up when soaked in water
column15: A gecko regrowing its lost tail
column16: A cut on a finger healing
column17: A 10-year-old growing taller
column18: Sperm cells being made in the testes
column28: Healing, growing, and regrowing a tail all need new, identical body cells made by mitosis. Sperm are made by meiosis, and a swelling raisin is just water moving in by osmosis, with no cells dividing.
column29: Look for examples where an organism needs more of the same kind of body cell.

column9: The M phase (division phase) of the cell cycle is made up of which two processes?
column14: Meiosis and fertilization
column15: DNA copying and cell growth
column16: Mitosis and cytokinesis
column17: G1 and S
column28: The M phase is when the cell actually divides: mitosis divides the nucleus and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. G1 and S, along with growth and DNA copying, are parts of interphase. A common mistake is thinking mitosis by itself makes two cells.
column29: One process splits the nucleus and the other splits the rest of the cell.

column9: Why do biology classes use the tip of an onion root to look for cells in mitosis?
column14: Cells near the tip of a growing root divide often, so many are caught in mitosis
column15: Onion root cells have the largest chromosomes of any living thing
column16: Onion root cells never go through interphase
column17: Onion cells have no cell wall, so the chromosomes are easy to see
column28: The tip of a root is where the root grows, so its cells divide often and many are in some phase of mitosis. Onion cells do have cell walls, and even root tip cells spend most of their time in interphase. A common mistake is thinking every cell on the slide will be dividing.
column29: Where does a root get longer?

column9: A student looks at an onion root tip slide using a 10× eyepiece (ocular) lens and a 40× objective lens. What is the total magnification? (Enter just the number, for example 50 for 50×.)
column28: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = 400×. A common mistake is adding the lenses (10 + 40 = 50) instead of multiplying.
column29: The two lenses magnify one after the other, so combine them by multiplying, not adding.

column9: When a cell divides by mitosis, the original cell is called the parent cell, and the two new cells are called ___ cells.
column28: The two new cells are daughter cells. They are identical to each other and to the parent cell. A common mistake is writing sister cells; 'sister' is used for the two halves of a chromosome, not for the cells.
column29: Think of a family word that goes with 'parent.'

column9: Looking at an onion root tip, a student sees a cell with one round, dark nucleus and no separate chromosomes visible. Which stage is the cell most likely in?
column14: Anaphase
column15: Prophase
column16: Metaphase
column17: Interphase
column28: A cell with a whole nucleus and no visible chromosomes is in interphase; its DNA is uncoiled, so it can't be seen as separate chromosomes. In every phase of mitosis the chromosomes are coiled up and visible. A common mistake is thinking the cell has no DNA at all.
column29: Are the chromosomes visible? If not, is the cell dividing?

column9: Your hair grows about 1 cm every month. Where does the new material for a growing hair come from?
column14: Cells at the base of the hair follicle divide by mitosis and push the hair up
column15: Hair cells go through meiosis to make new hair
column16: The tip of the hair grows longer on its own
column17: The hair absorbs water from shampoo and stretches
column28: Hair grows from the root. Cells at the base of the follicle divide by mitosis, and the new cells push older ones upward, where they harden into the hair you see. The tip is dead and does not grow. Saying hair grows from the tip is the common mistake.
column29: Think about where a hair is attached to your body, not the end you can see.

column9: Which of these cells divides by mitosis most often?
column14: A skin cell in the bottom layer of the epidermis
column15: A cell in the outer layer of dead skin
column16: An adult heart muscle cell
column17: A mature nerve cell in the brain
column28: Skin cells at the bottom of the epidermis divide constantly to replace the skin that rubs off. Mature nerve and heart muscle cells rarely divide, and dead skin cells cannot divide at all. A common mistake is thinking every body cell divides at the same rate.
column29: Which tissue is always being worn away and replaced?

column9: A class models a duplicated chromosome with two pipe cleaners of the same color, twisted together at one spot by a bead. In this model, what does the bead stand for?
column14: The centromere
column15: The cell membrane
column16: A spindle fiber
column17: The nucleus
column28: The bead joins the two identical pipe cleaners (the two copies of the chromosome), so it represents the centromere. Spindle fibers would be strings pulling on the chromosome, not the spot that joins it.
column29: What part of a real chromosome holds its two copies together?

column9: In a yarn model of mitosis, students tie strings from each end of the 'cell' to the chromosomes and use them to pull the chromosomes apart. What do the strings represent?
column14: Spindle fibers
column15: Chromatin
column16: The nuclear membrane
column17: Centromeres
column28: Spindle fibers stretch from the poles of the cell to the chromosomes and pull them apart, just like the strings. Centromeres are the joining spots on the chromosomes, which is where the strings would attach.
column29: What in a real cell reaches from the poles to the chromosomes?

column9: A human life begins as a single cell called a zygote. How does that one cell become a baby with trillions of cells?
column14: The zygote and its daughter cells divide by mitosis again and again
column15: The zygote divides by meiosis to make cells with half the DNA
column16: The mother's cells move into the embryo to fill it in
column17: The zygote just keeps growing until it is the size of a baby
column28: Development starts with the zygote dividing by mitosis. Every new cell divides again, so the number of cells doubles over and over. A cell cannot just grow huge, and meiosis is only for making sex cells.
column29: Each division doubles the number of cells. What process is doing the dividing?

column9: A single cell divides by mitosis, and then every new cell divides again. After 3 rounds of division, how many cells are there?
column28: Each round doubles the cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. A common mistake is multiplying 3 × 2 = 6 instead of doubling three times.
column29: Start with 1 and double it once for each round.

column9: Animal cells divide their cytoplasm by pinching in at the middle. Why can't plant cells do this?
column14: They have a stiff cell wall around the cell membrane
column15: They have no nucleus
column16: They have no cell membrane
column17: They have no cytoplasm
column28: The rigid cell wall keeps a plant cell from pinching in, so plant cells build a new wall across the middle instead. Plant cells do have a cell membrane, a nucleus, and cytoplasm. A common mistake is thinking plants lack a cell membrane.
column29: What does a plant cell have on its outside that an animal cell does not?

column9: A student wants to find lots of dividing animal cells to draw. Which slide would be the BEST choice?
column14: A thin slice of cork
column15: A slice of adult brain tissue
column16: A whitefish embryo (blastula), where cells are dividing quickly
column17: A strand of human hair
column28: An embryo is growing fast, so many of its cells are in mitosis at any moment. Adult brain cells rarely divide, and hair and cork are made of dead cells that cannot divide. A common mistake is thinking any animal tissue will show lots of mitosis.
column29: Which sample comes from something that is growing quickly?

column9: During interphase, a cell is resting and does no work.
column28: False. Interphase is a very busy time: the cell grows, makes proteins, does its normal job, and copies its DNA. It is only 'resting' from dividing. Calling interphase a resting stage is a very common mistake.
column29: Think about everything that has to happen before a cell is ready to divide.

column9: Why does a cell copy its DNA before it goes through mitosis?
column14: So that each daughter cell gets half of the DNA
column15: So that the cell can get rid of its old DNA
column16: So that the cell can make more energy
column17: So that each daughter cell gets a complete set of DNA
column28: Copying the DNA makes two full sets. Mitosis then gives one complete set to each daughter cell. Without copying first, each new cell would get only half, which is the common mistake in thinking.
column29: If you had to share one book with a friend and both of you needed the whole book, what would you do first?

column9: The cells lining your small intestine wear out and are replaced every few days. Which role of mitosis does this show?
column14: Replacing worn-out cells
column15: Asexual reproduction
column16: Making sex cells
column17: Growing a new organism from a zygote
column28: The intestine's lining is constantly scraped by food, so its cells are replaced by mitosis every few days. This is replacement (or maintenance). Asexual reproduction makes a whole new organism, and sex cells come from meiosis.
column29: Nothing new is being grown here. The body is swapping old cells for fresh ones.

column9: Which of these living things can carry out mitosis? Select all that apply.
column14: An amoeba
column15: A Streptococcus bacterium
column16: A housefly
column17: A mushroom
column28: Mitosis is division of a nucleus, so only eukaryotes (organisms whose cells have a nucleus) can do it. Amoebas, mushrooms, and houseflies are all eukaryotes. Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus; they divide by binary fission. A common mistake is thinking every living thing uses mitosis.
column29: Mitosis divides a nucleus. Which of these organisms have cells with a nucleus?

column9: A cell has two separate clumps of chromosomes at opposite ends, a faint nuclear membrane forming around each clump, and its cell membrane starting to pinch in at the middle. Which phase of mitosis is this cell in?
column14: Anaphase
column15: Metaphase
column16: Prophase
column17: Telophase
column28: New nuclear membranes forming around two groups of chromosomes means telophase, and cytokinesis often starts at the same time. In anaphase the chromosomes are still moving and there are no nuclear membranes yet. A common mistake is choosing anaphase because the chromosomes are at the ends.
column29: Focus on the nuclear membranes. Are they breaking down or being rebuilt?

column9: In a whitefish embryo cell, the chromosomes are thick and clearly visible, the nuclear membrane is gone, and the chromosomes are scattered around the cell, not lined up. Which phase is this cell in?
column14: Metaphase
column15: Telophase
column16: Anaphase
column17: Prophase
column28: Visible chromosomes with no nuclear membrane, but not yet lined up, means prophase (late prophase). Once they form a line in the middle it is metaphase. A common mistake is calling any cell with visible chromosomes metaphase.
column29: The chromosomes are visible but haven't been organized yet. Which phase comes before the lining up?

column9: Spindle fibers attach to each duplicated chromosome at which location?
column14: At the nucleolus
column15: At the two tips of the chromosome
column16: At the cell wall
column17: At the centromere
column28: Spindle fibers attach at the centromere (to protein patches there), so when the fibers pull, the two copies separate cleanly. They do not grab the tips. A common mistake is mixing up the centromere with the centriole, where spindle fibers start in animal cells.
column29: The fibers need to grab the spot that holds the two copies together.

column9: In an onion root tip, far more cells are found in interphase than in any phase of mitosis. What is the best explanation?
column14: Cells in mitosis are too small to see
column15: Mitosis only happens at night
column16: Interphase lasts much longer than any phase of mitosis
column17: Interphase cells are bigger, so they are easier to count
column28: A snapshot of a tissue catches more cells in long stages and fewer in short ones. Since interphase takes up most of the cell cycle, most cells are in interphase. A common mistake is thinking the root tip simply isn't growing.
column29: If you took a photo of a school at random times, where would most students be: in class or in the hallway?

column9: Put these events in the order they happen as a cell divides.
column14: The two copies of each chromosome move to opposite poles
column15: Two nuclei form and the chromosomes unwind
column16: The cytoplasm is split between two cells
column17: Long, thin DNA strands coil into thick, visible chromosomes
column18: Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell
column28: This is prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase → cytokinesis. The chromosomes must become visible and organized before they can be separated, and the nuclei form before the cell finishes splitting. A common mistake is putting cytokinesis before telophase.
column29: Name the phase for each event first, then use PMAT.

column9: A skin cell on your arm divides by mitosis. Which statements about the two new skin cells are true? Select all that apply.
column14: They are genetically identical to each other
column15: They have the same genes as the parent cell
column16: They each contain a mix of DNA from two different parents
column17: They have half as many chromosomes as the parent cell
column18: They have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell
column28: Mitosis copies and divides the DNA evenly, so both daughter cells have the same chromosome number and the same genes as the parent and as each other. Half the chromosomes and a mix of DNA describe meiosis and fertilization. Mixing up mitosis and meiosis is the most common mistake.
column29: Mitosis makes copies. Which statements describe copies?

column9: A cell finishes mitosis, but cytokinesis does not happen. What is the result?
column14: One cell with one nucleus that has half as much DNA
column15: One cell with two nuclei
column16: Two cells that each have no nucleus
column17: Two cells that each have half of a nucleus
column28: Mitosis already made two nuclei. Cytokinesis is what splits the cytoplasm to make two cells, so without it, one cell ends up with two nuclei. A common mistake is thinking mitosis by itself makes two cells.
column29: Mitosis divides the nucleus. What does cytokinesis divide?

column9: Why does a cell make extra organelles, such as mitochondria, before it divides?
column14: So that each daughter cell has the organelles it needs to survive
column15: Because extra organelles make the nucleus divide faster
column16: Because organelles make the cell's DNA
column17: Because organelles become the spindle fibers
column28: When the cell splits, its organelles are shared between the two daughter cells. Making extra ones first means each new cell has enough mitochondria and other parts to work. A common mistake is thinking only the DNA needs to be doubled.
column29: Each daughter cell has to be a working cell on its own.

column9: Why does a cell coil its DNA into compact chromosomes before dividing it?
column14: So the DNA can be moved and separated without tangling or breaking
column15: So the DNA can fit through the cell membrane
column16: So the DNA can be read to make proteins faster
column17: So the DNA can be copied
column28: Uncoiled DNA is extremely long and would tangle like loose string. Coiling it into chromosomes makes it compact enough to move and split evenly. DNA is copied while it is uncoiled, in interphase, which is the common mistake.
column29: Think about moving a long extension cord: is it easier when it's loose or wound up?

column9: A dog skin cell has 78 chromosomes. It divides by mitosis, and then both daughter cells divide by mitosis again. How many chromosomes are in each of the final cells?
column28: Every round of mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, so after two rounds each cell still has 78. The number of cells changes (1 → 2 → 4), but not the chromosomes per cell. A common mistake is halving the number each time.
column29: Count chromosomes per cell, not the number of cells.

column9: A hydra (a tiny freshwater animal) grows a small bud on its side. The bud breaks off and becomes a new hydra. Which role of mitosis does this show?
column14: Making sex cells
column15: Asexual reproduction
column16: Replacing worn-out cells
column17: Repairing an injury
column28: The bud forms by mitosis and becomes a whole new organism with the same DNA as the parent, which is asexual reproduction. Repair and replacement fix the same organism instead of making a new one. Sex cells come from meiosis.
column29: A new organism is made, and only one parent is involved.

column9: Match each example to the role of mitosis it shows.
column14: A corn seedling's stem gets taller and thicker :: Growth
column15: A broken leg bone heals :: Repair
column16: A fertilized egg becomes an embryo with many kinds of tissue :: Development
column17: A strawberry plant sends out a runner that roots and becomes a new plant :: Asexual reproduction
column28: Healing a bone is repair, a stem getting taller and thicker is growth, a runner making a new plant is asexual reproduction, and a fertilized egg becoming an embryo is development. A common mistake is calling the strawberry runner growth, but it makes a whole new plant.
column29: Ask: is it fixing damage, getting bigger, making a new organism, or building a body from one cell?

column9: As a cell grows larger, its volume increases faster than its surface area. Why is this a problem that dividing helps solve?
column14: The cell wall becomes too thin and breaks
column15: The cell runs out of DNA as it grows
column16: The cell membrane can't move enough food and oxygen in, and wastes out, for all that volume
column17: The nucleus becomes too small to see
column28: Everything a cell needs enters, and all its wastes leave, through its surface. A big cell has too little surface for its volume, so it can't keep up. Dividing into two smaller cells restores a high surface-area-to-volume ratio. A common mistake is thinking a cell divides because it 'runs out of room' for DNA.
column29: Where does everything enter and leave a cell?

column9: A cube-shaped cell is 2 µm on each side. Its surface area is 24 µm² and its volume is 8 µm³. What is its surface-area-to-volume ratio? (Enter one number, for example 5 for 5:1.)
column28: Surface area ÷ volume = 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so the ratio is 3:1. A common mistake is dividing volume by surface area (8 ÷ 24) instead.
column29: Surface area goes on top.

column9: Why is it important that the chromosomes line up in a single row across the middle of the cell before they separate?
column14: So that the chromosomes can uncoil
column15: So that a nuclear membrane can form around them
column16: So that each daughter cell receives exactly one copy of every chromosome
column17: So that the DNA can be copied
column28: Lining up in the middle, with fibers from both poles attached, makes sure that when the copies are pulled apart, one copy of every chromosome goes to each side. DNA is copied earlier, during interphase. A common mistake is thinking the line-up is just for show.
column29: What would happen if some chromosomes were not lined up when the pulling started?

column9: A student counts onion root tip cells and finds: interphase 160, prophase 20, metaphase 8, anaphase 4, telophase 8. Which phase of mitosis appears to be the shortest?
column14: Prophase
column15: Metaphase
column16: Telophase
column17: Anaphase
column28: The fewer cells caught in a phase, the shorter that phase lasts. Anaphase has the fewest cells (4), so it is the shortest. A common mistake is picking the phase with the most cells.
column29: A short phase is less likely to be caught in a snapshot.

column9: Which of these happen BEFORE metaphase begins? Select all that apply.
column14: The nuclear membrane breaks down
column15: The cytoplasm divides
column16: The DNA coils into visible chromosomes
column17: The DNA is copied
column18: The copies of each chromosome separate
column28: DNA is copied in interphase, and in prophase the chromosomes condense and the nuclear membrane breaks down, all before metaphase. Separating the copies (anaphase) and dividing the cytoplasm (cytokinesis) come after metaphase. A common mistake is thinking DNA is copied during mitosis.
column29: Line up the stages: interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis. Which events belong to the first two?

column9: A cell in G1 has a certain amount of DNA. Call it 1 unit. How much DNA does the same cell have in G2?
column14: 2 units
column15: 4 units
column16: ½ unit
column17: 1 unit
column28: The DNA is copied during the S phase, which comes between G1 and G2, so the amount doubles from 1 to 2 units. A common mistake is saying 1 unit because the number of chromosomes doesn't change.
column29: What happens to the DNA between G1 and G2?

column9: A student builds a clay model of metaphase with 4 chromosomes. Each chromosome is a single, unduplicated strand of clay. What is wrong with the model?
column14: At metaphase the chromosomes should be scattered randomly
column15: At metaphase there should be a nuclear membrane around the chromosomes
column16: At metaphase there should be 8 separate single chromosomes
column17: At metaphase each chromosome should be doubled, with two identical copies still attached
column28: The DNA was copied in interphase, so at metaphase every chromosome is a doubled X shape with its two copies joined. The copies don't separate until anaphase. A common mistake is drawing single strands at metaphase.
column29: Has the DNA already been copied by the time the cell reaches metaphase?

column9: A farmer plants pieces of one potato, each with an 'eye,' and each piece grows into a new plant by mitosis. The original potato plant resisted a certain disease. The new plants will most likely:
column14: Not resist the disease, because mitosis changes genes
column15: Have a 50% chance of resisting the disease
column16: Resist the disease only if they are crossed with another plant
column17: Also resist the disease, because they have the same DNA as the original
column28: Growing a plant from a potato eye is asexual reproduction by mitosis, so the new plants are clones with the same DNA and the same traits. A common mistake is thinking new plants always get a mix of traits, which only happens with sexual reproduction.
column29: Is any new DNA mixed in when a plant grows from a piece of the parent?

column9: A muscle cell and a skin cell in your body both came from the same zygote by mitosis. Why do they look and work so differently?
column14: Skin cells were made by meiosis
column15: Muscle cells lost some of their DNA
column16: They use (turn on) different genes from the same DNA
column17: They have different chromosomes
column28: Mitosis gives every body cell the same DNA. During development, cells specialize by turning on some genes and turning off others. A common mistake is thinking different cell types have different DNA.
column29: Same instruction book, different chapters being read.

column9: Skin stem cells growing in a lab dish divide by mitosis every 20 hours, and every new cell keeps dividing at the same rate. Starting with 1 cell, how many cells will there be after 100 hours?
column28: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 rounds of division. Doubling 5 times: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32. A common mistake is multiplying 5 × 2 = 10 instead of doubling 5 times.
column29: First figure out how many rounds of division fit in 100 hours, then double that many times.

column9: A student says, "During mitosis, each chromosome splits down the middle, so each daughter cell gets half of each chromosome." What is wrong with this idea?
column14: The chromosomes split during cytokinesis, not mitosis
column15: Chromosomes do not move at all during mitosis
column16: The two halves that separate are complete, identical copies made when the DNA was copied earlier, so each daughter cell gets a full copy of every chromosome
column17: Nothing; the student is correct
column28: A duplicated chromosome is two complete copies joined together. When they separate, each daughter cell gets a whole copy, not half. Thinking a daughter cell gets 'half a chromosome' is the misconception.
column29: Before the split, was each chromosome one copy or two?

column9: A student is shown a photo of a dividing cell and must decide whether it is a plant cell or an animal cell. Which observation is the BEST evidence that it is a plant cell?
column14: The chromosomes are lined up in the middle
column15: A cell plate is forming between the two new nuclei
column16: Two nuclei are forming
column17: Spindle fibers are present
column28: Only plant cells build a cell plate (a new wall) during cytokinesis. Lined-up chromosomes, spindle fibers, and two forming nuclei happen in both plant and animal cells, so they can't tell them apart. A common mistake is picking a feature both kinds of cells share.
column29: Look for something that happens in only one kind of cell.

column9: When a single-celled amoeba divides by mitosis and cytokinesis, what is the result?
column14: One larger amoeba
column15: Four sex cells that must join to make a new amoeba
column16: Two new amoebas that are genetically identical to the original
column17: Two amoebas that each have half of the original's DNA
column28: For a one-celled organism, dividing by mitosis is reproduction: one amoeba becomes two identical amoebas. A common mistake is thinking mitosis is only for growth and repair in many-celled organisms.
column29: If the whole organism is one cell, what happens when that cell divides?

column9: Students use pipe cleaners to model one cell cycle. Put their model steps in order.
column14: Line up the doubled pipe cleaners along the middle of the 'cell'
column15: Twist each pipe cleaner together with an identical copy
column16: Draw a line across the middle to split the 'cell' in two
column17: Pull one pipe cleaner from each pair to opposite sides
column18: Draw a circle around each group to show two new nuclei
column28: Copying the DNA (S phase) → lining up (metaphase) → pulling apart (anaphase) → new nuclei (telophase) → splitting the cell (cytokinesis). A common mistake is lining up the pipe cleaners before they've been copied.
column29: Each step in the model matches a real step. Start with the step that happens in interphase.

column9: A scientist growing human cells in a dish sees a cell with its chromosomes lined up in the middle. What will happen NEXT in this cell?
column14: The DNA will be copied
column15: The chromosomes will coil up and become visible
column16: The copies of each chromosome will separate and move to opposite poles
column17: The nuclear membrane will break down
column28: Chromosomes lined up in the middle means metaphase, and anaphase comes next, when the copies separate. The nuclear membrane breaking down and chromosomes becoming visible happen earlier, in prophase, and DNA is copied in interphase.
column29: Name the phase this cell is in, then think about which phase follows it.

column9: On a pie chart of the cell cycle, interphase takes up about 90% of the circle. If one cell cycle takes 20 hours, about how many hours does the cell spend in interphase?
column28: 90% of 20 hours = 0.90 × 20 = 18 hours. The other 2 hours are mitosis and cytokinesis. A common mistake is answering 2, which is the time spent dividing.
column29: Change 90% to a decimal and multiply by the total time.

column9: Which statement about mitosis in plant and animal cells is TRUE?
column14: Only animal cells go through anaphase
column15: Plant daughter cells end up with half as many chromosomes
column16: Both go through the same phases of mitosis but divide the cytoplasm differently
column17: Plant cells skip interphase
column28: Plant and animal cells both go through prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. The difference is in cytokinesis: animal cells pinch in, while plant cells build a new wall across the middle. A common mistake is thinking plant cells use a completely different process.
column29: Where in cell division does the cell wall make a difference?

column9: A student says that because no chromosomes can be seen in a cell during interphase, the cell must not have any DNA then. Which response is best?
column14: The DNA leaves the nucleus during interphase
column15: The DNA is there, but it is uncoiled and spread out, so it is too thin to see as separate chromosomes
column16: The DNA is stored in the cell membrane during interphase
column17: The student is correct; DNA is made only during mitosis
column28: During interphase DNA is loose and spread out so the cell can read and copy it, which makes it too thin to see as chromosomes. It coils up and becomes visible in prophase. Thinking 'invisible means missing' is the misconception.
column29: Can a cell do its job and copy its DNA without having any DNA?

column9: A cat body cell has 38 chromosomes in G1. After the DNA is copied, the cell enters G2. How many chromosomes does it have in G2?
column28: Copying the DNA doubles the amount of DNA, but each copy stays attached to the original at the centromere. So the cell still has 38 chromosomes, each made of 2 sister chromatids (76 chromatids). Answering 76 is the common mistake of counting chromatids as chromosomes.
column29: After copying, are the two copies separate chromosomes, or still joined as one?

column9: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. By metaphase, each chromosome is made of two identical halves joined together. How many of these halves are in the cell in total?
column28: Each of the 46 chromosomes is made of 2 sister chromatids, so 46 × 2 = 92 chromatids. The cell still counts as having 46 chromosomes. A common mistake is answering 46 or 23.
column29: Multiply the number of chromosomes by the number of halves each one has.

column9: A pea plant cell has 14 chromosomes. During anaphase, the two copies of each chromosome separate, and each copy now counts as its own chromosome. How many chromosomes are in the cell during anaphase, before cytokinesis?
column28: Each of the 14 doubled chromosomes splits into 2 separate chromosomes, so there are 28 in the cell for a short time. After cytokinesis each daughter cell gets 14, the same as the parent. A common mistake is answering 14 because that is the number in the daughter cells.
column29: Count after the split but before the cell divides into two.

column9: A scientist treats dividing cells with a chemical that stops spindle fibers from forming. Which outcome is most likely?
column14: The DNA cannot be copied during the S phase
column15: The cell divides normally, only faster
column16: The chromosomes condense but cannot line up or separate, so mitosis stops before anaphase
column17: The cell skips straight to cytokinesis and makes two identical cells
column28: Spindle fibers are needed to line chromosomes up and pull them apart. Without them, the chromosomes can still coil up in prophase, but the cell gets stuck and cannot reach anaphase. DNA copying happens earlier and does not need spindle fibers, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Which phases of mitosis depend on fibers pulling on the chromosomes?

column9: An onion root tip cell cycle takes about 24 hours. In a sample of 400 cells, 40 are in prophase. Assuming the share of cells in a phase matches the share of time that phase lasts, about how many hours does prophase last?
column28: 40 ÷ 400 = 0.10, so 10% of cells are in prophase. 10% of 24 hours = 0.10 × 24 = 2.4 hours. A common mistake is stopping at the percent (10) instead of multiplying by the cycle time.
column29: Find the fraction of cells in prophase first, then take that fraction of 24 hours.

column9: A student counts 250 cells in a root tip: 225 are in interphase and the rest are in mitosis. The whole cell cycle takes 16 hours. About how many MINUTES does mitosis last?
column28: 25 of 250 cells are in mitosis: 25 ÷ 250 = 0.10. 0.10 × 16 hours = 1.6 hours, and 1.6 × 60 = 96 minutes. A common mistake is forgetting to convert hours to minutes and answering 1.6.
column29: First find how many cells are in mitosis, then the fraction, then the time in hours, then convert to minutes.

column9: A cell has 6 units of DNA in G2. How much DNA will each daughter cell have right after cytokinesis?
column14: 3 units
column15: 12 units
column16: 6 units
column17: 1.5 units
column28: In G2 the DNA has already been doubled. Mitosis divides it evenly, so each daughter cell gets half of the G2 amount: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 units, the same as the parent had in G1. A common mistake is answering 6 because 'mitosis makes identical cells.'
column29: G2 has a doubled amount. What does each daughter cell get when it is divided evenly between two cells?

column9: A graph shows the amount of DNA in one cell over time. The line is flat, then rises slowly over several hours until it has doubled, stays high for a while, and then suddenly drops back to its starting level. What do the slow rise and the sudden drop show?
column14: The rise is mitosis; the drop is the S phase
column15: The rise is the DNA being copied in S phase; the drop is the cell dividing into two
column16: The rise is G1 growth; the drop is the DNA being destroyed
column17: The rise is prophase; the drop is metaphase
column28: DNA doubles during the S phase, which takes hours. The amount stays doubled through G2 and mitosis, then drops by half when cytokinesis splits the DNA between two cells. A common mistake is thinking mitosis makes the DNA.
column29: When is new DNA made, and when is it split between two cells?

column9: During anaphase, both copies of one chromosome are mistakenly pulled to the same pole. All other chromosomes separate normally. What is the result?
column14: Both daughter cells have one extra chromosome
column15: One daughter cell has an extra chromosome, and the other is missing that chromosome
column16: The cell makes four daughter cells instead of two
column17: Both daughter cells are normal
column28: If both copies go one way, that daughter cell gets an extra copy and the other gets none of that chromosome. This is why lining up and separating correctly matters. A common mistake is thinking the cell can 'fix' it by sharing.
column29: Follow the two copies of that one chromosome. Where does each end up?

column9: Suppose a cell went into mitosis without ever completing its S phase. What would be the main problem?
column14: It would make four daughter cells instead of two
column15: Its chromosomes would not have been copied, so the daughter cells could not each get a complete set
column16: It would turn into a sex cell
column17: Its nuclear membrane would never break down
column28: S phase is when the DNA is copied. Without it, there is only one set to divide, so the daughter cells would each get an incomplete set. A common mistake is thinking mitosis itself makes the extra DNA.
column29: What does the S phase do, and why does mitosis need it?

column9: A student claims, "The daughter cells from mitosis are identical to the parent cell in every way." Which is the best correction?
column14: They are genetically different from the parent cell
column15: They actually have only half of the parent cell's DNA
column16: The claim is completely correct
column17: They have identical DNA, but they start out smaller than the parent cell and must grow during G1
column28: The DNA is identical, but splitting one cell into two leaves each daughter cell smaller, with about half the cytoplasm and organelles. They grow back to full size in G1. A common mistake is accepting 'identical in every way' when only the DNA is identical.
column29: Think about size, not just DNA.

column9: Why can't a mature human red blood cell divide by mitosis?
column14: It has no nucleus, so it has no chromosomes to copy and divide
column15: It has too much DNA to divide
column16: It is too small to have a spindle
column17: It has a cell wall that blocks division
column28: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus as they develop, so there are no chromosomes for mitosis to divide. New red blood cells are made by stem cells in bone marrow instead. A common mistake is thinking human cells have cell walls.
column29: Mitosis is the division of what?

column9: Follow ONE chromosome through the cell cycle. Put these descriptions in order, starting in G1.
column14: An X shape lined up at the center with fibers attached from both sides
column15: A single strand uncoiling inside a new nucleus
column16: A single, uncoiled strand of DNA inside the nucleus
column17: A thick, coiled X shape that can be seen with a microscope
column18: Two separate strands being pulled toward opposite poles
column19: Two identical strands joined together, still uncoiled
column28: G1 (single, uncoiled) → S (copied, two strands joined) → prophase (coiled, visible X) → metaphase (lined up) → anaphase (copies pulled apart) → telophase (uncoiling in a new nucleus). A common mistake is putting the coiled X before the DNA has been copied.
column29: The X shape only exists after the DNA is copied.

column9: A student wants to estimate how long metaphase lasts in onion root tip cells. Which method would give the most reliable estimate?
column14: Watch one cell on a prepared slide for 5 minutes and time metaphase
column15: Measure how wide the metaphase cells are
column16: Count only the metaphase cells in one field of view
column17: Count cells in every phase across several fields of view, find the fraction in metaphase, and multiply by the total cell cycle time
column28: A large sample from several fields of view gives a reliable fraction, and that fraction times the cycle length estimates the time. Prepared slide cells are dead, so watching one won't work, and counting only metaphase cells gives no fraction to compare. A common mistake is using too small a sample.
column29: Cells on a prepared slide are not alive. How can a snapshot tell you about time?

column9: Compare a cell in G1 with the same cell in G2. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
column14: The G2 cell has twice as many chromosomes
column15: The G2 cell has twice as much DNA
column16: The G1 cell has thick, visible chromosomes
column17: Both have the same number of chromosomes
column18: In G2, each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids
column28: S phase doubles the DNA, but the copies stay joined, so the chromosome count is the same and each chromosome now has two sister chromatids. In both G1 and G2 the DNA is uncoiled, so no thick chromosomes are visible. Saying G2 has twice as many chromosomes is the most common mistake.
column29: Did the copies separate after S phase, or are they still joined?

column9: A student's model shows a cell in metaphase. Which features should the model include? Select all that apply.
column14: An unbroken nuclear membrane around the chromosomes
column15: Each chromosome made of two joined chromatids
column16: Chromosomes in a single line across the center
column17: Two separate nuclei at opposite ends of the cell
column18: Spindle fibers attached at the centromeres
column28: At metaphase the doubled chromosomes are lined up in the middle with spindle fibers attached at their centromeres. The nuclear membrane broke down in prophase, and two nuclei don't form until telophase. A common mistake is leaving the nuclear membrane in the model.
column29: Check each feature: has it happened yet at metaphase, or has it already gone away?

column9: A cell has 4 chromosomes in G1. Match each stage to what its chromosomes look like.
column14: G2 :: 4 doubled chromosomes, still uncoiled inside a nucleus
column15: Anaphase :: 8 single chromosomes moving toward the poles
column16: Metaphase :: 4 doubled chromosomes in a single line at the center
column17: Telophase :: Two groups of 4 single chromosomes, each with a new nuclear membrane forming
column28: After S phase the 4 chromosomes are doubled but uncoiled (G2), then line up (metaphase). In anaphase the copies split, so for a short time there are 8 single chromosomes, and in telophase each new nucleus gets 4. A common mistake is thinking the count is 8 in G2.
column29: The count only changes when the copies separate.

column9: Cell A is a cube 1 mm on each side. Cell B is a cube 3 mm on each side. Which statement is correct?
column14: Both cells have the same ratio because both are cubes
column15: Cell B has a ratio of 6:1, so it exchanges materials better than Cell A
column16: Cell A has a ratio of 1:6, so it is too small to survive
column17: Cell A has a surface-area-to-volume ratio of 6:1 and Cell B has 2:1, so Cell B has less membrane for each unit of volume
column28: Cell A: surface area 6 × 1² = 6 mm², volume 1³ = 1 mm³, ratio 6:1. Cell B: 6 × 3² = 54 mm², volume 3³ = 27 mm³, ratio 2:1. The bigger cell has less surface for its volume, which is why cells divide instead of growing huge. A common mistake is thinking a bigger cell has a better ratio because it has more surface area overall.
column29: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side × side. Volume = side × side × side.

column9: Starting with one fertilized egg, every cell divides by mitosis in each round. What is the smallest number of rounds needed to reach at least 1,000 cells?
column28: Doubling: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 after 9 rounds, and 1,024 after 10 rounds. A common mistake is choosing 9 rounds, which gives only 512 cells.
column29: Keep doubling from 1 and count how many times you double.

column9: Two onion root tips are compared. In Root A, grown in warm soil, 30% of the cells are in mitosis. In Root B, grown in cold soil, 10% are in mitosis. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Root A's cells have more chromosomes than Root B's cells
column15: Root A's cells are dividing more often, so Root A is probably growing faster
column16: Temperature has no effect on how often cells divide
column17: Root B is probably growing faster because its cells spend more time in interphase
column28: A higher percentage of cells in mitosis means more division is happening, which means faster growth. The data support that warmer soil sped up cell division in this case. A common mistake is thinking more time in interphase means more growth.
column29: Which root is making new cells more often?

column9: A parent cell has 4 doubled chromosomes. In a student's drawing of anaphase, each pole receives 2 whole X-shaped (doubled) chromosomes. What is wrong with the drawing?
column14: Each pole should receive 8 doubled chromosomes
column15: Each doubled chromosome should split, sending one copy of EVERY chromosome to each pole, so each pole gets 4 single chromosomes
column16: In anaphase the chromosomes should still be lined up in the middle
column17: Nothing is wrong; each pole should get half of the chromosomes
column28: In anaphase the copies of each chromosome separate, so every pole gets one copy of all 4 chromosomes. In the drawing, each daughter cell would be missing 2 chromosomes. Sending whole X shapes to the poles is the common mistake; in mitosis the X shapes always split first.
column29: Each daughter cell needs one copy of every chromosome, not half of the chromosomes.

column9: Right after fertilization, a frog embryo's cells divide very quickly, but the embryo as a whole does not get any bigger. What must be true?
column14: The cells are not copying their DNA
column15: The embryo's cells are dividing by meiosis
column16: Each division makes smaller cells, because the cells divide again without a growth period in between
column17: The cells are dying as fast as they divide
column28: In early embryos, cells skip most of the growth phase (G1) and divide over and over, so the cells get smaller with each division while the embryo stays the same size. The DNA must still be copied each time. A common mistake is thinking every division makes cells as big as the parent cell.
column29: If one cell becomes two and neither grows, what happens to their size?

column9: If a dividing cell's chromosomes lined up at the center, but the two copies of each chromosome never separated, the cell would be stuck in ___.
column28: Lining up in the center is metaphase. The next step, anaphase, starts when the copies separate, so if they never separate the cell stays stuck in metaphase. A common mistake is writing anaphase, but anaphase never begins.
column29: Name the phase where the chromosomes are lined up, then ask whether the cell can move past it.

column9: Some cancer drugs work by blocking mitosis. Patients taking them often lose their hair. What is the best explanation?
column14: The drugs make hair cells go through meiosis
column15: The drugs dissolve the hair that is already grown
column16: Hair is made of DNA, which the drugs destroy
column17: The drugs affect all fast-dividing cells, and hair follicle cells divide often to make hair
column28: Blocking mitosis hits any cells that divide often, including hair follicle cells, so new hair isn't made and hair falls out. Grown hair is not dissolved, and hair is made of protein, not DNA. A common mistake is thinking the drugs only affect cancer cells.
column29: Which normal body cells divide very often, like cancer cells do?

column9: A student says, "Mitosis makes new DNA." Which response is most accurate?
column14: Wrong: the DNA is copied before mitosis begins, during interphase, and mitosis only divides those copies between two nuclei
column15: Wrong: mitosis destroys half of the DNA
column16: Correct: mitosis is the process that copies DNA
column17: Wrong: DNA is copied during cytokinesis
column28: DNA replication happens in interphase. Mitosis separates the copies that already exist so each nucleus gets one full set. Thinking mitosis itself makes DNA is a very common mistake.
column29: When in the cell cycle is the DNA actually copied?
